We'll spend some time discussing the meaning behind the Jacobian shortly. But for now, let's get some practice at computing it.

Intuition Behind the Jacobian
?

The Jacobian determinant gives information about nonlinear transformations similar to that described by the determinant properties of affine transformations.

The critical difference is that, in general, the Jacobian describes local effects, not global ones.

To understand what this means, suppose that is a transformation, where

and we assume that and have continuous first-order partial derivatives on

For ease of notation, let's introduce to denote the Jacobian determinant of evaluated at

Let's describe 's effect on a tiny rectangle in the -plane whose bottom-left corner is the point

It's important to note that the image of our rectangle in the -plane is typically not a parallelogram! However, provided that our rectangle is very small, its image can be approximated by a parallelogram (we'll justify this in a future lesson).

The Jacobian determinant of evaluated at describes the following key features between our tiny rectangle and its (approximate) image:

  • The local area scale factor of .

    Suppose the length and width of our rectangle are and so its area is Then, it can be shown that the parallelogram in the -plane has an area equal to

    Note the similarity of this formula with that of affine transformations described earlier (we've simply replaced with the Jacobian).

    If the transformation is (locally) orientation-preserving.

  • Whether the transformation is locally invertible or locally non-invertible.

    Points such that are called critical points. Critical points are very important. We'll discuss these in more detail in future lessons.

We again stress that the Jacobian describes local properties, that is, local to the point The effect of a nonlinear transformation on an object varies as we move around the -plane, so its local properties also vary. So, for example, if a transformation is orientation-preserving at one point, it does not mean it's orientation-preserving everywhere!

The circulation Γ measures the total work done by a force F in moving a particle along a closed curve C. It is given by the formula Γ=∮CF⋅dr=∫abF(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.

Along the curve C, we have x=cos⁡(πt),y=sin⁡(πt),z=1−t2.

So,

Computing r′(t), we get

Therefore,

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve C representing the intersection of the paraboloid z=10−x2−y2 and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid S with the equation

z=g(x,y)=10−x2−y2.

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph z=g(x,y):

∂g∂x=∂∂x(10−x2−y2)=−2x∂g∂y=∂∂y(10−x2−y2)=−2y

Next, we substitute the equation z=g(x,y) into expression for curlF:

curlF|z=g(x,y)=⟨−2z,0,0⟩|z=10−x2−y2=⟨−2(10−x2−y2),0,0⟩=⟨2x2+2y2−20⏟P,0⏟Q,0⏟R⟩

So, we have

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA=∬D(−(2x2+2y2−20)⋅(−2x)−0⋅(−2y)+0)dA=∬D(4x3+4xy2−40x)dA,

where D is region enclosed by the projection of C onto the xy-plane, shown below.

∫C∇f⋅dr=f(r(b))−f(r(a)).

First, we define P(x,y) and Q(x,y) as follows:

F(x,y)=x1+x2+y2⏟P(x,y)i+y1+x2+y2⏟Q(x,y)j.

To apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we must first find a potential function f (if it exists) such that F=∇f. Notice that the domain of F is R2, and

∂P∂y=∂Q∂x=−2xy(1+x2+y2)2.

Since the partial derivatives are continuous and equal everywhere on R2, there exists a potential function f such that F=∇f, and we must have

fx(x,y)=x1+x2+y2,fy(x,y)=y1+x2+y2.

Reconstructing the function f from its gradient in the usual way, we get

f(x,y)=12ln⁡(1+x2+y2).

Note that we set C=0 for the arbitrary constant since we can use any function f that satisfies ∇f=F.

We're now ready to apply the fundamental theorem for line integrals. A suitable parametrization of the curve C is given by

r(t)=⟨t,t2ln⁡(t+1)⟩,t∈[0,1].

The position vectors of the endpoints of the curve are given by

r(0)=⟨0,0⟩,r(1)=⟨1,ln⁡2⟩.

Therefore, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path defined by C are (0,0) and (1,ln⁡2).

Finally, applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

If F is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that F represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of F across C represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by C:

  • If more water flows out through C than in through C (i.e., there is a net flow out through C), the flux is positive.

  • If more water flows in through C than out through C (i.e., there is a net flow in through C), the flux is negative.

  • If the net flow through C is zero then the flux equals zero.

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

  • Statement I is false, while statement II is true. From the diagram below we see that F acts perpendicular to n at every point on C. Therefore, there is no net flow of F through C.

    So, the flux of F across C is zero, and we must have ∮CF⋅nds=0.

  • Statement III is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on C in either case.

    So, the flux of F across −C is zero, and we must have ∮−CF⋅nds=0.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

A connected region D is simply connected if every simple closed curve in D can be contracted to a point.

A connected plane region D is simply connected if every simple closed curve in D encloses only points in D. In other words, the region does not contain any holes. Plane regions containing holes are not simply connected, since some simple closed curves cannot be contracted to a point:

Let's now examine our regions in turn.

  • Region I is simply connected. Indeed, it is the half-plane y≥x. So, it's a plane region without holes,

  • Region II is not simply connected since it's a plane region with a hole (containing all points of the circle x2+y2≤1).

  • Region III is not simply connected. The region contains all the points of R2 except those on the straight line y=−x. Thus, the region is formed by two disjoint half-planes and, therefore, is not even a connected region.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

  2. The flux of F across C is zero
  3. The flux of F across −C is zero

If F is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C.

To understand the flux intuitively, we imagine that F represents a stream of flowing water. The flux of F across C represents the net flow of water escaping the region bounded by C:

  • If more water flows out through C than in through C (i.e., there is a net flow out through C), the flux is positive.

  • If more water flows in through C than out through C (i.e., there is a net flow in through C), the flux is negative.

  • If the net flow through C is zero then the flux equals zero.

For an arbitrary closed curve, the outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

  • Statement I is false, while statement II is true. From the diagram below we see that F acts perpendicular to n at every point on C. Therefore, there is no net flow of F through C.

    So, the flux of F across C is zero, and we must have ∮CF⋅nds=0.

  • Statement III is true. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on C in either case.

    So, the flux of F across −C is zero, and we must have ∮−CF⋅nds=0.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."
